component.name: AppAttic
component.summary: Leftovers, stale apps, unused packages, and disk usage

description.p: AppAttic finds leftover data from uninstalled apps, unused installed software, unused distro and language packages, outdated versions, and large folders. Nothing is deleted until you review a script or confirm in the window. Disk usage can move a folder to Trash after you confirm.
The Linux window is Qt 6. Package-manager queries run on the host when installed as a Flatpak (flatpak-spawn --host). Named package updates wait for confirm. Full distro upgrades are not run.

appattic restore is new. It puts settings.json.bak back in place of settings.json after checking that the backup loads, so an invalid or unreadable file changes nothing on disk; the file it replaces is preserved as settings.json.bad. It runs before regular settings are read, so it works on a system whose settings.json no longer parses. --json FILE writes the restore result as JSON. In the desktop windows, the Settings page adds a corresponding "Restore settings from backup" action.

A backup of the configuration is written to settings.json.bak by every settings save that changes the file, keeping the previous valid state. Saves that leave settings unchanged skip the backup so an older copy cannot be overwritten by a no-op save.

Outdated reporting explicitly identifies report-only packages. Footers and skip notes name language globals (npm, pnpm, Bun, pip, pipx, uv, RubyGems, Composer, Deno) alongside the App Store and Snap as report-only rows that are excluded from appattic update.

File permissions and path handling are hardened. Generated cleanup scripts and configuration backups are written owner-only (0600) to prevent visibility or races in shared temp directories. XDG root path normalization trims trailing separators consistently across the scan engine, the C host, and the Linux Qt interface.

A JSON report target has to name a .json file. --json scan and --json /var are usage errors now, exit 2, where the first wrote whatever the argument named and the second failed late against a directory: appattic --json erase used to write a file named erase and never erase anything. Name the file you want, --json scan.json.

A disk path has to name a path: it carries a separator (appattic disk /var, appattic disk ../other), it is . or .., the two directories every shell starts in, or it is a name that starts with a dash and came behind -- (appattic disk -- -backup). A bare word is exit 2 rather than a walk of a root that does not exist, and an empty argument, which is what a shell hands over for an unset variable, is exit 2 wherever it appears. appattic disk Desktop is the one to spell differently: appattic disk ./Desktop.

--version wins over a usage error anywhere on the line again, and now says so: 2.0.0 made a bad token elsewhere swallow it, and appattic --nope --version is exit 0 printing the version once more. --help still wins over it, so appattic --version --help prints the help.

A --category value that names a command is refused instead of used as a filter, so appattic --category erase reports that the filter needs a value and still reads erase as the command. Every other value is unchanged: a substring match against the name, path, root, and status, repeated as often as you like.

The deprecated positional-tuple brewPackageMeta(_:) is removed, as 2.0.0 said it would be. Call brewPackageMeta(from:) and read its named summaries and titles maps, which is the only form that says which map is which.

The scan reads foreign files more carefully. An os-release line written ID = ubuntu now yields the key ID rather than ID , so a lookup by name finds it. A flatpak row whose application id carries whitespace is not read as an app. A history line with a stray carriage return in the middle of a command is read the same by both history scanners, so which of the two runs no longer depends on whether some unrelated byte of the file is non-ASCII, and a command indexed twice carries the same time on both paths. A recently-used.xbel or application_state file carrying a processing instruction with no data at all, <?x?>, which is what a truncated writer leaves behind, used to take the process down inside the XML reader; it is read around. In the Linux window, an XDG root of / resolved a finding to //applications/…; it names the path the scan looked at again.

A Linux app row names the .desktop entry the scan found instead of the Exec binary it launches, a shared system binary that a removal could only ever be skipped for, so the cleanup line removes the launcher and the row shows the file whose size it reports. Ages read in the unit that fits again: two to three weeks, then months, then years, where weeks used to run to sixty days and a year started only at eighteen months. A generated upgrade guard no longer splices a redirect into the query it wraps, so the guard is the if <present>; then <action>; fi shape the specification documents. A --top or --category handed no value is refused on a command that ignores it, where only a flag that carried a value was.

The settings file is kept before it is replaced. settings.json.bak holds the last state the app itself wrote, so an emptied, truncated, or hand-mangled file is one cp away from being put back; a scan cannot rebuild it, because the ignore list is your own choice. Nothing reads the backup while AppAttic runs, and a backup that does not land does not stop the write you asked for. appattic config names the path and says whether it is there.

man appattic ships for the scan CLI, beside the appattic-qt page the Linux window already had. It documents the commands, the flags and the commands each belongs to, the exit codes, the environment variables, and the files the app writes.

An XDG root that ends in a separator names the directory the scan looked at again, so XDG_CONFIG_HOME=/srv/config/ and XDG_CONFIG_HOME=/srv/config are one path to the CLI, to the Linux window, and to the core host. appattic config prints the root it resolves to, which is now the XDG_RUNTIME_DIR the Linux window opens gvfs at as well. APPATTIC_CORE_OUT is read the same way: set but empty, padded, or relative is ignored and the directory is searched next to the binary, so a padded value cannot send the window looking where the plugins are not.

A flag that names one command is now a usage error on every other one instead of a silent no-op. Put --leftovers-only and --stale-only after report, --allocated and --all-file-systems after disk, --top N after report, leftovers or disk, --category after report or leftovers, and --include-system, --fresh and --dry-run after the commands appattic --help lists. --yes still belongs to update alone. A script that passed one of these to a command that ignored it used to exit 0 and now exits 2, so move the flag to the command it names. A bare appattic --allocated is one of those: with the command left out the default is report, so name disk.
--category takes one value and is repeated, so --category caches browser is a usage error where it used to filter on both. Pass --category caches --category browser.

--version used to print the version and exit 0 even when the rest of the line was wrong, and --help lost to it. It now reports the usage error and exits 2, and --help wins, so appattic --version --help prints the help. appattic help [command] is new as a word: appattic help disk prints what appattic disk --help prints. A bare -- ends the options, so appattic disk -- -backup scans a folder whose name starts with a dash instead of calling it an unknown option. With several wrong tokens on one line, the first one is the error reported.

appattic update asks on a terminal and stops with exit 2 when there is none, unless the run passes --yes. A cancelled update exits 1, where it used to exit 0. A disk path that is not a readable directory is a usage error rather than an empty report. An upgrade script that is still running after ten minutes is stopped and reported as exit 124, where it used to wait for the package manager to finish.
appattic config is new. It scans nothing: it prints the settings file this machine resolved, whether it exists, every setting with the layer it came from, and the paths the XDG variables resolved to.

appattic erase is new, and it is the one command that deletes: it removes the stored scan snapshot, a full list of the paths the last scan found under your home directory, whatever its age, and reads nothing first to decide. It reports on stdout whether a snapshot was there, with your home path redacted, and --json FILE writes the same as JSON. It runs before settings.json is read, so it still works on a machine whose settings no longer parse, and it leaves settings.json alone.

A finding under a configured XDG root was shown as a path under your home directory, so the row named a directory the scan never looked at. The Linux window shows the root the variables resolved to instead. A folder or package name carrying terminal control characters is printed with them stripped as well, where a name could rewrite a line of a report in your terminal.

An ignored leftover path in settings.json has to be the full path a report prints. A relative one, a ~ one, or one with a trailing slash matched nothing and hid nothing, so it is refused now, with the offending entry named: the CLI exits 2 and both windows open with no settings and say which entry to fix. The file is left exactly as it is, so correcting that one entry is the whole fix. The Linux window likewise no longer overwrites old settings that are neither true nor false with the defaults. It names the key and the old settings file, and opens with no settings until that file is corrected, because saving the defaults over your value would destroy it. A migration that lands in settings.json deletes the old file, so the ignore list in it is not left in a second copy nothing opens, and a migration that could not be written leaves it, since it is then the only copy.

Generated cleanup scripts quote plugin names and paths, and a name containing a newline can no longer inject shell. Each package removal is now guarded by a check that the package is still there, so running a script twice no longer fails on what the first run removed, and only the part of a command that needs root asks for it. Your home path is redacted from error and status messages. Non-ASCII names, case folding, and date, size, and duration formatting follow the locale, which replaces the English today and 3 days ago and the yyyy-MM-dd date with your locale's own. The last-scan cache records the exact mtime of what it scanned, is dropped after a run that removes or updates something, and is dropped once it is over 24 hours old. A scan in which any check ran and failed is not saved, so a failed package query is retried on the next run instead of being served as "no unused packages" for a day. A snapshot that does not decode is deleted on the spot rather than read again on every launch. settings.json, last-scan.json, and every temporary file the app creates are now made owner-only from the start instead of being narrowed after the write, so there is no window in which another account on the machine can read the app and leftover paths they hold.

A folder size could read smaller than it is: du exits non-zero when a path it was asked about failed, and a batched run counted the partial total it still printed as a real measurement. A bind mount that loops back into its own tree also spun the walk out to its deadline instead of finishing. Both are fixed, and Java, Gradle, Maven, and .m2 are recognized as system paths, so they are no longer offered as leftovers. Disk usage ranks the entries in each folder by the size it prints, by apparent size unless --allocated asked for allocated blocks, so --top N no longer cuts the wrong rows.

A Homebrew formula holding 50 MB or more of user data, or data whose size could not be measured, is REVIEW and not REMOVE when the span of its history is all the usage evidence there is. A cleanup script that used to remove such a formula does not any more, and the row says why.

A PPA entry whose name was not a plain file name could put a path outside /etc/apt/sources.list.d into a generated cleanup script. Such a name is refused now, alongside the newline-injection fix above.
The Linux window ships a man page: man appattic-qt.

One library entry point is deprecated in this release: the positional-tuple brewPackageMeta(_:), whose two maps are told apart only by their order. It now warns at compile time and goes in 3.0.0. brewPackageMeta(from:) names them and is the replacement.

The AppImage carries update information pointing at the .zsync published beside it, so a downloaded copy can check for a newer release with AppImageUpdate. The Flatpak did not build at all: the wasmtime headers and the zig toolchain were removed from the build before the app window needed them, and the icon and the desktop entry were renamed on top of the ids the package already had. Both build now, under one desktop id and its own icon.
The AppImage ran only on the machine that built it: the bundled wasmtime recorded an absolute build path as its dependency, so a downloaded AppImage failed to start anywhere else.
Findings, disk folders, and the disk ring now appear as each plugin reports instead of after the whole scan finishes.
A date or version that cannot be read shows as unknown rather than an empty value.
The findings table is painted from a model rather than rebuilt, a rescan that returns the same findings no longer rebuilds it, and column widths are sampled instead of measured for every row.
Scans reuse the compiled WASM module and the wasmtime compilation cache across runs, a first scan starts faster, and a rescan saves about 60 ms.
The results table fills in roughly half the time, and search and filter toggles show or hide rows instead of rebuilding them.
Package-manager queries run in parallel, the byte-scan parsers were rewritten, and the grouping and probe fixes land with search debounce and the audit cleanups.
Disk usage builds on macOS again.
Disk usage, Linux distro cleanup, and portable package support.
The cache is invalidated after a same-name app update or a clock rollback, Homebrew cleanup is safe to rerun, and home paths no longer leak into generated scripts.
The offscreen Qt platform plugin is now shipped inside the AppImage, so every page renders without a display server.
First release: the Linux Qt window packaged as an AppImage, and the appattic scan CLI behind it.
